tooling-foundations:
:::details Practical evidence chain — browser failure → portable reproduction
Use Chrome DevTools when the symptom is visible in the browser but you need evidence that another engineer can replay.

1. Open DevTools → **Network**.
2. Turn on **Preserve log** if the failure crosses a navigation or reload.
3. Reproduce the failure and select the relevant request.
4. Inspect **Headers**, **Payload**, **Response**, and **Timing** before drawing a conclusion.
5. Right-click the request → **Copy → Copy as cURL** to create a portable reproduction. For a multi-request trace, export a **sanitized HAR**.
6. Re-run the cURL command outside the browser and compare the result with the original browser request.

Chrome documents both **Copy as cURL** and sanitized HAR export. Review any artifact before attaching it to a ticket.

[Official Chrome DevTools Network reference](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/network/reference/)
:::
http-api-tools:
:::details Real Postman walkthrough — Postman Echo → collection → assertion
This follows Postman’s current official quick start rather than a fictional API.

1. Open the Postman desktop app and click **Add** to open a request tab.
2. Enter `postman-echo.com/get` and click **Send**. Postman displays the Echo response in the response pane.
3. Click **Save → New Collection**, name the collection, then click **Save**.
4. Open **Scripts → Post-response**.
5. Open **Snippets** and choose **Status code: Code is 200**. Postman inserts this assertion:

```javascript
pm.test("Status code is 200", function () {
    pm.response.to.have.status(200);
});
```

6. Click **Send** again, then open **Test Results** in the response section.

![Postman request builder showing the Postman Echo response](https://assets.postman.com/postman-docs/v12/send-first-request.png "Official Postman Docs screenshot: request builder and response pane.")

[Official Postman quick start](https://learning.postman.com/docs/getting-started/quick-start/)
:::
browser-devtools:
:::details Real Chrome workflow — capture and replay a failing API request
1. Open DevTools → **Network**.
2. Enable **Preserve log** if navigation would otherwise clear the request list. Enable **Disable cache** only when you specifically want a first-load/no-cache reproduction.
3. Reproduce the issue and select the request.
4. Inspect **Headers**, **Payload**, **Response**, and **Timing**.
5. For an XHR request, right-click → **Replay XHR** to send it again without repeating the full UI interaction.
6. For a portable artifact, right-click → **Copy → Copy as cURL**. For a trace, use **Save all listed as HAR (sanitized)**.

![Chrome DevTools selected request Headers view](https://developer.chrome.com/static/docs/devtools/network/reference/image/request-headers.png "Official Chrome DevTools screenshot: selected network request and Headers tab.")

**Interpretation rule:** a copied request is evidence of what the browser sent, not proof of root cause. Compare the replay result with the UI symptom and server-side evidence.

[Official Chrome DevTools Network reference](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/network/reference/)
:::
interception-proxies:
:::details mitmproxy setup flow — capture authorized test traffic
Use this only on test systems and traffic you are authorized to inspect.

1. Start `mitmproxy`. In regular mode the documented default proxy is `http://localhost:8080`.
2. Configure the browser/device to use that HTTP(S) proxy.
3. Browse to `http://mitm.it` through the proxy and follow mitmproxy’s platform instructions for the test client.
4. Verify that the expected test traffic appears as flows in mitmproxy.
5. Select a flow and inspect the request and response to compare them with the browser/app symptom.
6. Record the proxy mode, client, target environment, request timestamp, and the specific flow used as evidence.

[Official mitmproxy getting started](https://docs.mitmproxy.org/stable/overview/getting-started/) · [Official proxy modes](https://docs.mitmproxy.org/stable/concepts/modes/)
:::
database-inspection:
:::details DBeaver investigation flow — read first and make production writes difficult
A SQL client can answer whether persisted state agrees with API/UI evidence, but the investigation itself should not accidentally mutate live data.

1. In **Database Navigator**, select the intended connection and verify its environment.
2. Open an SQL editor for that connection and begin with a narrow `SELECT` using deterministic identifiers and a sensible result limit.
3. Compare returned IDs, status fields, timestamps, and relationships with the API/UI evidence.
4. Check the connection’s transaction behavior. For an existing connection: right-click it → **Edit Connection → Connection settings → Initialization**. DBeaver exposes **Auto-commit** there.
5. Use an environment-specific **Connection type**. Current DBeaver defaults define **Production** with AutoCommit off and confirmations for SQL execution/data changes, while new connections use **Development** unless changed. Verify the actual connection rather than assuming its type.
6. If you only need evidence, stop after the read.

[Official DBeaver initialization settings](https://dbeaver.com/docs/dbeaver/Configure-Connection-Initialization-Settings/) · [Official DBeaver connection types](https://dbeaver.com/docs/dbeaver/Connection-Types/)
:::
packet-analysis:
:::details Real Wireshark flow — isolate one protocol conversation
1. Open the capture and select one packet from the connection you want to investigate.
2. Choose **Analyze → Follow** and select the applicable protocol stream. The same action is available from the packet-list context menu.
3. Wireshark applies the appropriate display filter for that stream and opens a dialog showing the conversation data.
4. Use the isolated stream together with packet timing and connection state to investigate where the observed behavior occurs.

![Wireshark Follow TCP Stream dialog](https://www.wireshark.org/docs/wsug_html/images/ws-follow-stream.png "Official Wireshark User’s Guide screenshot: Follow TCP Stream.")

[Official Wireshark User’s Guide — Following Protocol Streams](https://www.wireshark.org/docs/wsug_html_chunked/ChAdvFollowStreamSection.html)
:::
mobile-diagnostics:
:::details Android practical flow — identify device → reproduce → isolate Logcat evidence
1. Run `adb devices -l` and confirm the exact device/emulator serial and state.
2. Build/run the app on that target.
3. In Android Studio open **View → Tool Windows → Logcat**.
4. Start with `package:mine`. Add `level:ERROR` when you need errors and above, or use `is:crash` for application-crash entries. `is:stacktrace` is useful when the log level alone is not enough.
5. Reproduce the issue and record the device, app/build version, exact action, timestamp, and relevant stack trace/log sequence.

```text
package:mine & (level:ERROR | is:crash)
```

[Official Android Studio Logcat guide](https://developer.android.com/studio/debug/logcat) · [Official adb guide](https://developer.android.com/tools/adb)
::: 

:::details iPhone/iPad practical flow — live device logs in macOS Console
1. Connect the iPhone or iPad to the Mac.
2. Open **Console** on macOS and select the connected device in the **Devices** list.
3. Click **Start** to stream log messages.
4. Reproduce the problem and note the exact time.
5. Inspect errors/faults and message details around the reproduction time.

[Apple Console User Guide — View log messages](https://support.apple.com/guide/console/cnsl1012/mac)
:::
specialist-bridges:
:::details Practical handoff — give the specialist replayable evidence
When an investigation crosses into another specialty, preserve the artifact from the layer where the symptom was observed:

- **API/integration:** reproducible request plus status, response excerpt, and environment.
- **Browser/network:** sanitized HAR or copied request plus the exact UI reproduction step.
- **Database:** read-only query and the returned identifiers/timestamps used for reconciliation.
- **Packet analysis:** capture file, display filter, affected stream, and reproduction timestamp.
- **Mobile:** device/OS/build identifiers plus the focused Logcat or Console excerpt.

The goal is to let the next engineer reproduce the same observation without reconstructing your local state.
:::
